affo.title: AFFO
affo.content:
AFFO (adjusted funds from operations) is a property owner's distributable cash: net income excluding revaluations, adjusted for maintenance capex and lease incentives.

For Equinix, Inc.: the valuation capitalises AFFO at the cost of equity; statutory net income is dominated by revaluation noise.

What to watch:

  • AFFO per share growth
  • Payout ratio (DPS / AFFO per share)

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Equinix, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Equinix, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Equinix, Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Equinix, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Equinix, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Equinix, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Equinix, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Equinix, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Equinix, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Equinix, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue

revenueMix.title: Revenue by product line
revenueMix.content:
Equinix splits recurring revenue into Colocation (cabinet and power rental), Interconnection (cross-connects and fabric services between tenants), Managed Infrastructure (bare metal and managed services) and a smaller Other recurring line.

For Equinix, Inc.: Interconnection is the smallest line by dollars but the highest-margin and the one the "platform equinix" ecosystem thesis depends on — it grows from network density (more tenants, more cross-connects per cabinet), not just floor space. Colocation dominates revenue and tracks cabinet growth directly.

What to watch:

  • Interconnection growing faster than Colocation (density effect strengthening)
  • Managed Infrastructure's share of the mix — it is lower-margin and more competitive than core colocation

cabinetUtilization.title: Cabinet utilization
cabinetUtilization.content:
Cabinet utilization is billed cabinets as a percentage of available capacity — the occupancy rate of a data-center REIT, the direct analogue of occupancy for an office or retail landlord.

For Equinix, Inc.: utilization has drifted down from the low-80s to the high-70s as new capacity (Americas and Asia-Pacific builds) has come online faster than it has filled, which is the main reason revenue growth has outpaced per-cabinet pricing rather than pure occupancy gains. A region sustained below the others for several years signals oversupply or weaker local demand.

What to watch:

  • A falling trend alongside rising capacity (new builds not yet leased)
  • Which region is dragging the overall number down

dataCenterCount.title: Data center count by region
dataCenterCount.content:
The number of operating data centers in each region — the physical footprint behind the cabinet and revenue figures.

For Equinix, Inc.: Americas has the most sites but EMEA and Asia-Pacific have grown their counts faster recently, consistent with management's commentary that international markets are the larger greenfield opportunity. New sites take years to fill, so count growth is a leading indicator of future capacity, not current revenue.

What to watch:

  • Count growth outrunning utilization (capacity built ahead of demand)
  • Regional mix shifting the long-run growth and margin profile

bookings.title: Annualized gross bookings
bookings.content:
Annualized gross bookings is the annualized value of new and expansion leases signed in the quarter — a forward indicator of revenue, reported before churn and net of nothing.

For Equinix, Inc.: because recurring revenue recognizes over the life of a lease, bookings growth today is the best read on revenue growth one to two quarters out, ahead of it showing up in Colocation or Interconnection revenue.

What to watch:

  • Bookings growth decelerating or reversing before revenue growth does
  • Large single-quarter swings from one hyperscale deal

mrrPerCabinet.title: MRR per cabinet by region
mrrPerCabinet.content:
Monthly recurring revenue (MRR) per cabinet is the average monthly price realized per billed cabinet in each region — the pricing/mix KPI, separate from the occupancy KPI above.

For Equinix, Inc.: Americas commands the highest MRR per cabinet, with EMEA the fastest grower recently as mix shifts toward larger, power-dense deployments (AI/cloud) that command a premium over standard retail colocation.

What to watch:

  • MRR per cabinet rising even as utilization is flat or falling — pricing power/mix offsetting occupancy
  • Regional convergence or divergence in pricing

customerConcentration.title: Customer concentration
customerConcentration.content:
The share of recurring revenue from the single largest customer and from the top 50 customers combined.

For Equinix, Inc.: concentration is low and has stayed roughly flat (largest customer around 2-3% of recurring revenue, top 50 around 36%) despite a large and growing customer base — a structural strength versus REITs or networks dependent on a handful of anchor tenants.

What to watch:

  • A rising trend, which would signal growing reliance on a few large (often hyperscale) tenants
  • Any step change coinciding with a disclosed large deal
